text: The Taliban published an 11-page biography of Mullah Mohammed Omar, apparently to counter rumors that its reclusive leader is dead. The document portrays Omar as still directing the movement, amid rising pressure from ISIS and questions over Taliban leadership.

Hundreds mourned Walter Scott at a South Carolina funeral, where speakers called his fatal police shooting a catalyst for change. Former North Charleston officer Michael Slager has been charged with murder after video showed him shooting Scott as he ran away.

Former TSA agent Daniel Boykin was sentenced to six months in jail and 5½ years’ probation for secretly filming a female co-worker and entering her home to collect images and data. Prosecutors said police found more than 90 videos and 1,500 photos of the victim; TSA said Boykin was fired when the investigation began.

Cape Verde is looking to its rich musical heritage to drive economic growth and boost tourism, with festivals and industry events promoting local artists abroad. Officials and private promoters say music can raise the island nation’s global profile at lower cost than traditional marketing.

Arsenal beat Burnley 1-0 through Aaron Ramsey to stay second and move within four points of Premier League leaders Chelsea, who have two games in hand. Aston Villa boosted their survival hopes by beating Tottenham, while Leicester and Crystal Palace also earned key wins in the relegation fight.

Original Twin Peaks cast members launched a #SaveTwinPeaks video campaign backing David Lynch in his salary dispute with Showtime. Lynch quit the planned 2016 revival, though Showtime says it still hopes to bring him back.

Andrew Getty, grandson of oil tycoon J. Paul Getty, appears to have died of natural causes at his Los Angeles home, police said. Authorities said there was no sign of foul play, though an autopsy is pending.

A Maryland woman accused of leaving her quadriplegic son in Philadelphia woods for days cannot be extradited until she completes unspecified treatment, police said. The 21-year-old, who has cerebral palsy, was found dehydrated and malnourished in Cobbs Creek Park; his mother faces assault and endangerment charges.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer has named an asteroid after Malala Yousafzai, the Pakistani education activist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate. Asteroid 316201 Malala orbits between Mars and Jupiter and honors her advocacy for girls’ education.

A gastrointestinal illness has sickened 100 people aboard Celebrity Cruises’ Infinity, the CDC said. The cause is unknown, and CDC staff will meet the ship in San Diego as the cruise line steps up cleaning and testing.

“Star Wars” hit digital HD, Mindy Kaling’s brother claimed he posed as black to enter medical school, and actor James Best of “Dukes of Hazzard” died. Other viral moments included Burger King funding a Burger-King couple’s wedding, Michelle Obama dancing at the Easter Egg Roll, and Nina Dobrev leaving “The Vampire Diaries.”

The FBI charged Philadelphia woman Keonna Thomas with trying to travel overseas to join ISIS, citing social media posts and travel plans through Turkey and Spain. She is one of three women arrested this week on terror charges, including two New York women accused of plotting to build a bomb.
HBO released a teaser for Season 2 of “True Detective,” premiering June 21. The new season stars Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams and Taylor Kitsch in a California-set murder conspiracy.

Carlos Colina, 32, was charged after human remains were found in a duffel bag and at an apartment building in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Authorities identified the victim as Jonathan Camilien, 26, who knew Colina, and said more charges could follow pending medical examiner findings.

Louisville basketball recruit Trey Moses asked freshman Ellie Meredith, who has Down syndrome, to be his prom date in a gesture that went viral. Teachers and family praised the invitation as a boost for inclusion efforts at Eastern High School.

NBC debuts “A.D. The Bible Continues,” a sequel to History’s hit “The Bible,” as part of a crowded TV week. Other premieres and returns include the final “Mad Men” episodes, “American Odyssey,” “Louie,” “The Comedians” and Netflix’s “Marvel’s Daredevil.”

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence’s religious freedom law has ignited backlash while boosting his standing with social conservatives. The fight is pulling 2016 Republican hopefuls toward a harder line on LGBT rights, despite broader national support for same-sex marriage.

Apple’s latest mobile update adds more diverse emojis, including multiple skin tones, same-sex couples and new flags. The changes drew praise for broader representation, though some groups, including redheads and Armenians, said they were still excluded.

Avril Lavigne says she was bedridden for five months after contracting Lyme disease, ending speculation over her absence from music. The singer told People she is now “80 percent better” and plans to release a single supporting the 2015 Special Olympics.

New research from the Anne Frank House suggests Anne Frank and her sister Margot died of typhus at Bergen-Belsen at least a month earlier than previously believed. The study cites survivor testimony and archives indicating they likely died in February 1945, not March.

Two Troy University students were arrested on charges of gang raping a woman during spring break in Panama City Beach, Florida. Authorities identified the victim from a video found during an unrelated investigation and said more arrests are expected.

A stray dog in Washington state survived being hit by a car, apparently struck with a hammer and buried, later staggering to a farm four days later. Theia, now in veterinary care, needs surgery for jaw, leg and sinus injuries, with donors surpassing a $10,000 fundraising goal.

The FBI confirmed Malaysian bomb maker Zulkifli bin Hir, known as Marwan, was killed in a January raid in the southern Philippines. The operation left 44 elite police commandos dead and has threatened a fragile peace process with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.

A Republican critic says Obama is conceding too much leverage in the Iran nuclear framework, arguing sanctions forced Tehran to negotiate and should have been tightened. He warns the deal leaves Iran’s nuclear infrastructure intact, gives it major sanctions relief and lacks tough inspections to prevent cheating.

“Mad Men” begins its final episodes Sunday, closing a series that became a cultural touchstone despite modest ratings. The article speculates the show will track the late-1960s unraveling through agency upheaval, shifting social mores and Don Draper’s unresolved isolation.

Katie the giraffe gave birth to a roughly 6-foot-tall calf at the Dallas Zoo in a labor streamed live online by Animal Planet. The newborn’s gender and condition were not immediately known, but early signs included movement, attempts to stand and nursing efforts.

Loretta Lynch’s nomination to become the first African-American woman U.S. attorney general has stalled for a historically long period before a Senate vote. Republicans deny race is a factor, citing partisan fights over immigration and trafficking legislation, while Lynch’s supporters in North Carolina allege discrimination and press senators to act.

Three people were killed and five wounded when armed assailants stormed the attorney general’s office in Afghanistan’s Balkh province. Afghan security forces were engaged in an ongoing firefight as they advanced cautiously to avoid civilian casualties.
Bob Barker returned to "The Price Is Right" for the first time in eight years on the show's April 1 episode. The 91-year-old former host led the opening game before handing duties back to Drew Carey.

Blues legend B.B. King, 89, was hospitalized for dehydration linked to Type II diabetes but has been released and is resting at home. His daughter said King is “much better,” and the guitarist thanked fans for their concern.

A CNN opinion piece argues the Tsarnaev verdict underscores the need to understand Muslim radicalization without blaming Islam itself. It says extremists exploit real grievances facing Muslims, and prevention depends on offering young Muslims constructive civic engagement instead of violence.

CNN highlighted its top videos of the week, including a tour of Mike Tyson’s abandoned Ohio mansion, a ride on Carowinds’ Fury 325 coaster and an interview on allegations against Bikram Choudhury. Other clips featured a witness to the Germanwings crash, debate over Indiana’s religious freedom law and a study on facial attractiveness.

Coalition forces have retaken 25-30% of Iraqi territory seized by ISIS, the Pentagon said, with gains mainly along the group’s front lines. An analyst said the losses hurt ISIS’ image but the group is shifting to asymmetric attacks and battles such as Ramadi to project momentum.

A passenger on an Air Canada flight to Atlanta allegedly tried to choke Ottawa Fury soccer player Oliver Minatel with a headphone cord, witnesses said. The flight landed safely and the suspect was taken for medical and mental evaluation, with no federal charges pending.

A Hong Kong court adjourned until May a hearing for Briton Rurik Jutting, charged with murdering two Indonesian women found in his Wan Chai apartment. The former banker was deemed fit to enter a plea as authorities analyze extensive forensic and DNA evidence.

Tornadoes swept across the rural Midwest, killing one person in Fairdale, Illinois, and causing widespread damage in nearby Rochelle and Ogle County. Officials said warnings likely saved lives as homes, roads and businesses were destroyed across the region.
Don McLean’s handwritten lyrics for “American Pie” sold for $1.2 million at Christie’s. The 16-page manuscript includes drafts, unused lines and notes for the 1972 No. 1 hit.

UNRWA chief Pierre Krähenbühl will make an emergency visit to Syria’s Yarmouk refugee camp amid concern for 18,000 civilians trapped by fighting. The camp, largely cut off from aid since 2013, is mostly controlled by ISIS and Al-Nusra Front, with reports of hunger, medical shortages and government barrel bomb attacks.

Saudi-led airstrikes hit Houthi targets in Yemen’s capital Sanaa, crippling infrastructure and cutting power to millions. Nearly 600 people have been killed in fighting, prompting the Red Cross to seek a humanitarian ceasefire and urgent aid access.

Former Australia cricket captain and famed broadcaster Richie Benaud has died aged 84 after being treated for skin cancer. Tributes poured in for the former Test great, who captained Australia without losing a series and became one of cricket’s most iconic voices.

A total lunar eclipse early today will be visible across much of North America, with the best views in the West. NASA says totality will last just 4 minutes and 43 seconds, making it the shortest lunar eclipse of the century.

A federal grand jury charged real estate heir Robert Durst with illegally possessing a .38-caliber revolver found in his New Orleans hotel room. Durst, already held without bail on murder, weapons and drug charges, also faces extradition to Los Angeles in the 2000 killing of Susan Berman.

“Furious 7” opens Friday as both a franchise sequel and a tribute to Paul Walker, who died in a 2013 car crash during production. Filmmakers rewrote the script, used effects and his brothers as doubles to complete his role, while co-stars and fans continue to honor the actor.

A model on “The Price Is Right” accidentally revealed the winning answer, handing a contestant a new Hyundai Sonata. Host Drew Carey laughed off the mistake, and model Manuela Arbelaez later said everything was OK.

Thai Smile unveiled an “Adventure Time”-themed Airbus A320 in Bangkok, featuring characters from the Cartoon Network show inside and out. The livery promotes a partnership with Cartoon Network Amazone water park, with the first flight set for April 4 from Bangkok to Phuket.
Pedestrians in downtown Washington stopped traffic to help a mother duck and her ducklings cross busy L Street NW in the rain. The duck family was guided to a safer grassy area.

French investigators have collected the main evidence from the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site and do not expect to return. Authorities say co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately caused the crash, which killed all 150 people aboard.

Cuba will attend the Summit of the Americas for the first time since 1962, marking a milestone in its thaw with the United States. Washington and Havana may use the Panama forum to advance talks on restoring diplomatic ties, though Cuba’s place on the U.S. terrorism list remains a key obstacle.

Jesus and his followers likely survived on hospitality, begging and donations while living at subsistence level, scholars say. The article highlights wealthy backers, especially women such as Mary Magdalene and Joanna, whose resources helped sustain Jesus’ ministry.

California regulators ordered PG&E to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty over unsafe gas pipeline operations tied to the 2010 San Bruno explosion that killed eight people. Most of the penalty will fund pipeline safety improvements, as PG&E apologized and said it is working to regain public trust.

Lauren Hill, the 19-year-old college basketball player whose fight against brain cancer inspired millions, has died. Hill played for Mount St. Joseph after the NCAA moved up its opener, and helped raise $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research.

A large fire broke out Friday morning at GE’s Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky, sending thick smoke over the area. Authorities said no injuries or trapped people were reported, and the cause was not yet known.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif has become a prominent figure in nuclear talks with the U.S., drawing praise at home after a breakthrough framework. Less-known details include his U.S. education, past revolutionary activism, disputed birth date, and a previously alleged but unsettled link to a foundation accused of evading sanctions.

A Connecticut judge ruled that 17-year-old Cassandra C. must remain in state custody while completing court-ordered chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. The teen is in remission, and officials say she may return home after her final treatment later this month.

Researchers say computer analysis shows “Double Falsehood,” published in 1728, was largely written by William Shakespeare with contributions from John Fletcher. The study found little evidence that publisher Lewis Theobald authored the play, though some scholars remain skeptical.

French authorities said they were unaware of any onboard video from Germanwings Flight 9525, despite reports by Bild and Paris Match claiming a cellphone captured the crash’s final moments. Lufthansa confirmed co-pilot Andreas Lubitz had disclosed a past episode of severe depression during training, as investigators probe whether fear of losing his license contributed to the crash.

A decorated U.S. veteran born in American Samoa is challenging the federal government’s denial of citizenship to people born in the territory. The lawsuit asks the D.C. Circuit to extend birthright citizenship to American Samoans, arguing their exclusion rests on discredited, racist legal precedents.

Blue Bell temporarily shut its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, plant after listeria was found in ice cream linked to the facility. The CDC warned consumers and institutions not to eat certain 3-ounce Blue Bell products from the plant as investigations continue into illnesses and deaths possibly tied to the company’s products.

Al-Shabaab claimed an attack on Garissa University College in eastern Kenya that killed many people and left others hostage. The assault underscores the Somali militant group’s expanding regional threat and Kenya’s worsening security challenges. Lasting stability, analysts say, will require addressing deeper political, economic and social grievances fueling recruitment.

The U.S. will complain to Moscow after a Russian SU-27 intercepted a U.S. RC-135U reconnaissance plane over the Baltic Sea in what the Pentagon called an unsafe maneuver. Russia said the U.S. aircraft was approaching its border with its transponder off, a claim U.S. officials denied.

A black-winged angel artwork appeared near the North Charleston site where Walter Scott was fatally shot by police and has become a Black Lives Matter symbol. Creator Phillip Hyman said he made the piece from reclaimed wood as an act of mourning and protest.

Video of Officer Michael Slager fatally shooting unarmed Walter Scott exposed contradictions in police accounts of the incident. Slager, who claimed Scott took his Taser, has been fired and charged with murder after footage showed him shooting Scott as he ran away.

ISIS claimed it seized parts of Iraq’s Baiji oil refinery after a weekend assault, posting images of clashes and smoke. Iraqi officials denied the claim, saying government forces remained in full control of the strategic facility.

Nashville’s district attorney barred prosecutors from offering female sterilization in plea deals after public backlash. The article argues such deals may be constitutional if voluntary, but says outrage may reflect gender bias because sterilization of male offenders has long drawn less scrutiny.

The Ebola epidemic has infected more than 25,000 people and killed over 10,000, exposing major gaps in global public health systems. New cases have fallen to their lowest weekly level since May 2014, but Guinea still faces unsafe burials and hidden transmission risks.

The NCAA says it has no legal duty to ensure athletes receive a legitimate education, despite long promoting academics as central to college sports. The stance comes in a lawsuit by former UNC athletes over the school’s academic fraud scandal, drawing accusations of hypocrisy from critics.

Six people were injured after an explosion at a controversial chemical plant in Zhangzhou, China, sparked a major fire. Authorities said the blast followed an oil leak at a storage facility, with no toxic spill reported, and the fire is now under control.

A CNN opinion piece says video of Officer Michael Slager fatally shooting Walter Scott underscores the need for police body cameras. The author argues cameras could deter misconduct, rebuild public trust and expose racial bias in law enforcement while broader reforms take longer.

The Summit of the Americas was set to spotlight a historic Obama-Castro encounter after the U.S.-Cuba thaw. But U.S. sanctions on Venezuelan officials and President Nicolás Maduro’s coup accusations have shifted attention to a broader regional clash.

A Russian nuclear submarine under repair caught fire at the Zvyozdochka shipyard in northwestern Russia. Officials said its reactor fuel and weapons had been removed, no one was injured, and the fire posed no threat.

Tropical storm Maysak, locally called Chedeng, approached the Philippines with winds over 70 mph, prompting warnings for flash floods and landslides. Authorities ordered evacuations and barred coastal activities ahead of expected landfall Sunday in Isabela province.

Deion Sanders publicly chided his son on Twitter for claiming he only eats “hood doughnuts.” The NFL legend reminded Deion Sanders Jr. of his trust fund, condo and clothing line, telling him to “stop the hood stuff.”

Guatemala faces epidemic levels of violence against women, driven by postwar impunity, organized crime and entrenched machismo. Despite new femicide laws, specialized courts and NGO efforts, advocates say most cases still go unpunished and millions of women remain at risk.

Police in Malegaon, India, are requiring cattle owners to submit photos and identifying details of their animals to help enforce Maharashtra’s beef ban. The move follows a cow slaughter case and comes amid protests from beef traders and criticism over restrictions on food choice.

Police in Lucknow, India, have bought drones equipped with cameras and pepper spray for use against violent protests and mob attacks. The plan has drawn criticism from those who warn it could suppress free speech and reflects an overly forceful approach to crowd control.

Don McLean’s handwritten “American Pie” lyrics sold at Christie’s for $1.2 million to an unnamed buyer. The 1971 anthem, inspired in part by the deaths of Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and the Big Bopper, remains one of America’s most enduring pop songs.

London’s Hatton Garden vault raid bore the hallmarks of a meticulously planned, old-style heist, likely involving inside information, specialist criminals and months of preparation. Investigators will focus on forensic evidence, CCTV, criminal networks and the handling of stolen cash, gold and jewels.

7-Eleven is holding its first Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day at participating U.S. stores Saturday. Customers can fill sanitary containers that fit a 10-inch display hole for $1.49, the price of a medium Slurpee.

Former Kentucky state Sen. Georgia Powers criticized Rand Paul’s presidential launch, saying his record undermines his outreach to minority voters. She cited his past questioning of civil rights and voting rights protections, opposition to the Education Department and immigration safeguards, and said his views are “outdated” and disqualifying.

A Lamborghini crashed into a guardrail at Walt Disney World Speedway’s Exotic Driving Experience, killing passenger Gary Terry, 36. Driver Tavon Watson, 24, was hospitalized with minor injuries after losing control, authorities said.

Aaron Hernandez’s defense rested after less than a day, following months of prosecution testimony in his murder trial over Odin Lloyd’s 2013 killing. Jurors will weigh largely circumstantial evidence, including disputed video, footwear and witness testimony, before deliberations begin after closing arguments.

China has formally detained women’s rights activist Wu Rongrong and four others for “creating disturbances” after they planned an anti-sexual-harassment protest. The case comes as Beijing prepares to advance a domestic violence law and mark the 20th anniversary of a landmark women’s rights conference. Critics say the detentions reflect a broader crackdown on independent activism.

Martin O’Malley said Hillary Clinton’s status as the “inevitable” Democratic frontrunner could collapse, citing past primary upsets. The possible 2016 contender urged a competitive Democratic primary, while stopping short of directly attacking Clinton.

Former NFL player Aaron Hernandez was convicted of first-degree murder in the 2013 killing of Odin Lloyd and sentenced to life in prison. Lloyd’s family described him in court as a devoted son, brother and athlete, while his mother said she forgave those involved in his death.

Ted Cruz opened his Iowa presidential campaign push with a heavy appeal to evangelical voters, emphasizing religious liberty, faith and social conservative issues. His strategy aims to unite evangelicals, tea party activists and libertarian-leaning Republicans in a crowded 2016 GOP field.

Marvel unveiled new looks at Vision in “Avengers: Age of Ultron” and Daredevil’s red suit ahead of their upcoming releases. Fox also revealed Ben Hardy as Angel in “X-Men: Apocalypse” and Jamie Bell’s CGI Thing in the “Fantastic Four” reboot.

Italy’s Coast Guard rescued 978 migrants Friday off Libya as crossings from Africa and the Middle East continue to surge. More than 10,000 migrants reached Italy in early 2015, while at least 480 have died in the Mediterranean this year, the IOM said.

TV5Monde began restoring broadcasts and social media access after what its director called an “extremely powerful” cyberattack crippled its 11 channels, websites and accounts. ISIS imagery appeared on the French-language network’s social media, but no group immediately claimed responsibility.

David Lynch says he will no longer direct Showtime’s planned 2016 revival of “Twin Peaks,” citing insufficient funding to make the series as needed. Showtime said it was saddened by the decision but still hopes to revive the show with Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost involved.

Key trials in Massachusetts near verdicts as juries weigh charges against Boston Marathon bombing suspect Dzhokhar Tsarnaev and ex-NFL player Aaron Hernandez. Rand Paul launched his presidential bid, while voters in Chicago and Ferguson head to closely watched local elections.

Tornadoes were reported in Kansas and Missouri as severe storms brought hail, flooding and wind damage. Forecasters warned more dangerous storms were expected Thursday across parts of the Midwest, Mississippi and Tennessee River valleys, and the southern Great Lakes.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without parole for the 2008 murder of ex-boyfriend Travis Alexander. A judge imposed the sentence after two juries deadlocked on whether Arias should receive the death penalty.

EPA tests found methyl bromide in a U.S. Virgin Islands villa where a Delaware family fell seriously ill after a nearby fumigation. Authorities, including the Justice Department, are investigating Terminix and possible violations of pesticide laws.

A Columbia Journalism School review found Rolling Stone’s retracted UVA gang-rape story resulted from sweeping reporting and editing failures. Legal experts say UVA likely cannot sue for defamation, but Phi Kappa Psi members may have a case if they can prove individual harm and damages.

FBI agents arrested Kevone Charleston, 36, after a chase and shooting outside a CVS in Forsyth County, Georgia. Authorities say Charleston is suspected in 32 commercial robberies; two agents were injured in crashes and later released, while Charleston’s wounds were not life-threatening.

An Alaska Airlines flight from Seattle to Los Angeles returned shortly after takeoff after passengers and crew heard banging from the cargo hold. A ramp agent who had fallen asleep inside was found unharmed; the airline is investigating.

A North Carolina judge ruled that Craig Hicks can face the death penalty in the killings of three Muslim college students in Chapel Hill. Hicks, charged with three counts of first-degree murder, has said little publicly as authorities examine whether the shootings stemmed from a parking dispute or a possible hate crime.

Amnesty International urged Afghan authorities to protect women’s rights activists, saying they face attacks from militants, warlords and officials while perpetrators often go unpunished. The report follows the mob killing of Farkhunda in Kabul, which sparked rare public protests by women demanding an end to violence and impunity.

A New York judge allowed divorce papers to be served via Facebook private message, highlighting the rise of online legal notification. The article argues digital service may be more reliable than older alternatives like publication notices or papers nailed to doors.

The Rev. Robert H. Schuller, founder of the “Hour of Power” TV ministry and Crystal Cathedral megachurch, has died at 88 after battling esophageal cancer. The California televangelist helped pioneer televised Sunday services with an upbeat “possibility thinking” gospel, but his ministry later collapsed amid family succession disputes and bankruptcy.

Four workers were killed and 45 injured in a major fire on Pemex’s Abkatun Permanente oil platform off Mexico’s coast. About 300 people were evacuated, and the blaze was extinguished after hours, with Pemex reporting no collapse or oil spill.

Kansas enacted the first U.S. law banning a common second-trimester abortion procedure, dilation and evacuation, with exceptions for the mother’s life or health. Supporters called it a landmark anti-abortion measure, while opponents said it endangers women and is among the nation’s most restrictive laws.

CCTV host Bi Fujian apologized after a video showed him cursing Mao Zedong while joking at a private dinner. The clip sparked a backlash and debate online in China, where public criticism of top leaders remains taboo, and CCTV said it would investigate.

Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized after a hot mic caught him using a slur about Wisconsin’s Frank Kaminsky following Kentucky’s Final Four loss. Kaminsky said Harrison called to apologize and that he considered the matter closed.
"Arrested Development" is set to return for a fifth season with 17 episodes, executive producer Brian Grazer said. Netflix declined to comment, and it was unclear whether the full cast will return.

CERN’s Large Hadron Collider restarted after a two-year shutdown, with proton beams circulating again in its 17-mile ring. Scientists hope the upgraded machine will probe Big Bang conditions, dark matter and other gaps in particle physics as it ramps up to record energy levels.

An Iranian observation aircraft flew within 50 yards of a U.S. Navy helicopter over the Persian Gulf, alarming U.S. officials who feared the maneuver could have escalated. Officials said the incident may have been ordered locally and are considering a formal protest to Tehran.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts in the Boston Marathon bombing trial, including 17 capital charges. The case now moves to a penalty phase, where jurors will decide whether he should be sentenced to death.

Indian police arrested four FabIndia employees after minister Smriti Irani spotted a security camera overlooking a store changing room in Goa. The outlet was sealed, officials were summoned, and the staff face voyeurism and privacy charges.

Iran plans to ease its post-1979 ban on women attending men’s sporting events, allowing “women and families” into some stadiums within a year. Officials indicated the change may apply mainly to indoor sports, amid growing pressure from international sports bodies.

Satyam founder Ramalinga Raju and nine others were sentenced to seven years in prison over India’s biggest corporate fraud scandal. Raju, who admitted in 2009 to a $1.6 billion accounting fraud, was also fined $804,000.

Alaska Airlines apologized after removing cancer patient Elizabeth Sedway from a Hawaii-to-California flight over medical concerns because she lacked a doctor’s note. The airline refunded her family’s tickets and paid for accommodations after the delay caused her to miss chemotherapy.

Kayahan, one of Turkey’s most beloved singers and songwriters, died of cancer Friday in Istanbul at 66. Best known for his love songs, he rose to fame with his 1991 album “I Made a Vow” and recorded nearly 20 albums.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu criticized the Iran nuclear framework, saying world powers should increase pressure for a better deal rather than accept it or go to war. Obama administration officials defended the pact, while U.S. lawmakers split along partisan lines over whether it sufficiently curbs Tehran’s nuclear ambitions.

A suspected domestic kidnapping led to linked shootings at the U.S. Census Bureau in Maryland and on Washington’s H Street, authorities said. A security guard was critically wounded, and the suspect and a police officer were injured in a shootout after a chase; the kidnapping victim was found safe.

Chelsea Manning, serving a 35-year sentence for leaking classified documents, has joined Twitter through dictated posts relayed by a communications firm. Manning, who lacks prison Internet access, said she hopes the account will be a two-way conversation.

Rapper Nelly was arrested in Tennessee after state troopers stopped his tour bus and reported finding methamphetamine, marijuana, drug paraphernalia and handguns. He was charged with felony drug possession and later posted bond.

A Delaware father is improving but his two sons remain critical after the family fell ill at a rented villa in St. John, possibly from methyl bromide pesticide exposure. The EPA and Justice Department are investigating whether the banned indoor fumigant was improperly used at the resort.

Online journalists across Asia face mounting legal pressure, censorship and imprisonment as governments target bloggers and digital media critics. In countries with weak rule of law, such as Bangladesh, online writers have also been attacked or killed with little accountability.

Nina Dobrev said she will leave “The Vampire Diaries” at the end of its sixth season, prompting backlash from fans. Many questioned continuing the CW series without her and worried her exit would derail the Elena-Damon storyline.

ISIS’s assault on Damascus’ Yarmouk camp has deepened a yearslong siege and bombardment that has left civilians trapped without adequate food, water or medicine. About 18,000 residents remain amid shelling, street fighting and scarce aid access, as U.N. officials urge greater international action.

NASA scientists say advances in telescopes and exoplanet surveys could reveal signs of primitive life beyond Earth within decades. But despite billions of potentially habitable planets, the odds of communicating with intelligent aliens remain remote.

Carlos Colina, 32, of Massachusetts, faces murder charges after Jonathan Camilien’s remains were found in a duffel bag and at a nearby Cambridge apartment building. Authorities said the two men knew each other; Colina had earlier been charged with assault and improper disposal of a body.

Kanye West settled a civil lawsuit with paparazzi photographer Daniel Ramos over a 2013 LAX assault and apologized as part of the deal. Terms were not disclosed; West had previously pleaded no contest to misdemeanor battery.

Obama’s push for an Iran nuclear deal is driven by political legacy concerns, weakening U.S. leverage, the article argues. The framework leaves Iran’s nuclear infrastructure largely intact while easing sanctions too soon, alarming regional allies and raising proliferation fears.

The fatal police shooting of Walter Scott in South Carolina has renewed scrutiny of police use of force and the role of bystander video in exposing disputed accounts. The article argues the U.S. has failed to enforce a 1994 law requiring comprehensive Justice Department data on police killings, leaving the scale and patterns of the problem largely unknown.

Five Americans monitored at an Omaha hospital after Ebola exposure in Sierra Leone have been released, with none developing the virus. They had contact with a Partners in Health colleague now being treated at the NIH, where the worker is in fair condition.

Mark Ronson’s “Uptown Funk!” featuring Bruno Mars topped the Billboard Hot 100 for a 13th week, the longest No. 1 run of the 2010s and tied for the 10th-longest in chart history. Natalie La Rose’s debut hit “Somebody,” featuring Jeremih, entered the top 10, while Maroon 5’s “Sugar” and Ed Sheeran’s “Thinking Out Loud” held at Nos. 2 and 3.

CNN highlights “Rex Manning Day,” an April 8 tribute to the 1995 film “Empire Records,” while noting other movie-famous dates. The list includes “Titanic” on April 14, “Miss Congeniality” on April 25, “Mean Girls” on October 3 and “Back to the Future Part II” on October 21, 2015.

Nicole Kidman’s critically panned “Grace of Monaco” will bypass U.S. theaters and premiere on Lifetime on May 25. The Weinstein Co. sold the film to the network after poor overseas results and long-running disputes over its cut and release.

Tokyo’s Shibuya ward approved “partnership certificates” for same-sex couples, granting limited rights such as hospital visitation and joint tenancy agreements. The move, Japan’s first such municipal recognition, is seen by activists as a step toward broader marriage equality despite conservative opposition.

California’s four-year drought is driving mandatory water cuts and threatening higher U.S. food prices, with the state supplying much of the nation’s produce. The wider Western drought has also pushed up beef prices and disrupted tourism, though California wine production remains strong.

The University of Michigan will proceed with a campus screening of “American Sniper” after reversing an earlier cancellation prompted by student objections. Officials said canceling the film conflicted with the school’s commitment to free expression, while offering “Paddington” as an alternative.

The 2015 MTV Movie Awards mixed standout moments from Amy Schumer, Channing Tatum, Rebel Wilson and musical performers with several awkward misfires. Highlights included Schumer’s opener, Tatum twerking for Jennifer Lopez and Robert Downey Jr.’s Avengers tribute, while weak spots ranged from an archery gag gone wrong to uneven jokes and speeches.

A 20- to 30-foot section of a fiberglass boat, suspected debris from Japan’s 2011 tsunami, was towed into Newport, Oregon, after drifting more than 4,000 miles. Biologists found yellowtail jack fish inside but said the invasive-species risk was low; the fish will go to the Oregon Coast Aquarium.

One year after Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok, more than 200 remain missing. Nigeria’s President-elect Muhammadu Buhari vowed to intensify the fight against the militants, while global calls to #BringBackOurGirls continued.

The article explains Holy Week and the Easter Triduum as a progression from suffering on Good Friday to uncertainty on Holy Saturday and resurrection on Easter Sunday. It argues the ritual reflects a universal human pattern of loss, transition and renewal.

Kenya froze 86 accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters after the Garissa university massacre killed 147 people. The move comes amid criticism of the government’s response, as Kenya mourned the victims and continued operations against the militant group.

Jia Jiang’s “100 Days of Rejection” project, launched after his startup was denied funding, went viral after a Krispy Kreme manager fulfilled his unusual donut request. His new book, “Rejection Proof,” argues that embracing rejection can reduce fear, build confidence and create opportunity.

Attorney General Eric Holder reminded Justice Department employees that soliciting prostitution is banned, even where it is legal, warning violations could bring suspension or firing. The memo follows an inspector general report citing DEA agents’ misconduct overseas involving prostitutes paid by drug cartels.

Authorities are investigating whether the fatal shooting of Wayne Community College employee Ron Lane was a hate crime. Suspect Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, a former work-study student, was arrested in Daytona Beach after allegedly fleeing North Carolina.

Amnesty International said governments increasingly used the death penalty in 2014 as a response to terrorism, crime and political instability. Executions fell globally to 607, excluding China, but Pakistan, Iran, Iraq, Egypt and Nigeria saw troubling increases in use or sentences.

A Duke student admitted to hanging a noose from a tree near a campus student union and is no longer on campus, university officials said. The incident sparked protests and remains under campus and criminal investigation.

Richard Dysart, the Emmy-winning actor best known as Leland McKenzie on NBC’s “L.A. Law,” has died at 86 after a long illness. A veteran of stage, film and television, Dysart also appeared in “The Thing,” “Being There,” “Pale Rider” and the Broadway production of “That Championship Season.”

Christians marked Easter with services at the Vatican and in Jerusalem, as Pope Francis urged peace in global conflict zones. The holiday’s shifting date is tied to moon phases and the vernal equinox, while traditions such as eggs and the Easter bunny trace largely to post-medieval German customs.

Chris Rock tweeted photos documenting three police traffic stops in seven weeks, reviving debate over racial profiling and “driving while black.” The posts drew support and criticism, while actor Isaiah Washington sparked backlash by suggesting Rock “adapt” to avoid police attention.
Bob Burns, Lynyrd Skynyrd’s original drummer, died Friday in a single-car crash in Cartersville, Georgia. He was 64 and was not wearing a seat belt, authorities said.
A cat-on-stairs photo has gone viral, sparking debate over whether the animal is going up or down. The optical illusion recalls #TheDress and has drawn advertisers into the online frenzy.

The U.S. and its P5+1 partners reached a framework deal to curb Iran’s nuclear program through reduced enrichment capacity and expanded inspections. The author argues critics rely on flawed claims about the deal’s aims, scope and enforcement, and says Congress should judge it on security merits.

Rolling Stone’s retracted UVA gang-rape story has overshadowed ongoing investigations into the university’s handling of sexual assault cases. Advocates say the discredited account sparked needed reforms but fear the fallout could deter victims from coming forward.

Indiana Pacers forward Chris Copeland was stabbed outside a New York nightclub and hospitalized in stable condition. Atlanta Hawks players Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha, not involved in the stabbing, were arrested on obstruction and disorderly conduct charges at the scene.
Twisted Sister said its 2016 tour, marking the band’s 40th anniversary, will be its last. Mike Portnoy will replace late drummer A.J. Pero, with two tribute shows planned in Pero’s honor.

John Travolta dismissed HBO’s critical Scientology documentary “Going Clear,” saying he has not seen it and has no interest in doing so. The actor said Scientology has been a positive force in his life, crediting it with helping him cope with the death of his son.

“Furious 7” opened to a record $146 million and drew emotional reactions for its tribute to late star Paul Walker. Filmmakers used doubles and CGI to complete his scenes, choosing to retire his character rather than kill him off.

HBO’s “Game of Thrones” returns Sunday with its highest-profile premiere yet, airing simultaneously in 170 countries. Season five is expected to converge major storylines, push beyond George R.R. Martin’s books in places and build toward bigger battles and higher stakes.

CNN recounts rare survival stories of people stranded at sea for days to more than a year, relying on rainwater, raw fish and makeshift repairs until rescue. The cases include sailors, fishermen and a tsunami survivor, underscoring both the peril and improbability of such rescues.

The first six "Star Wars" films arrive on digital HD Friday with new special features. Extras include behind-the-scenes looks at sound design, including how animal noises helped create the Geonosians’ alien voices.

Boston Marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts tied to the 2013 attack and its aftermath. Survivors and victims’ families called the verdict a step toward accountability and closure, while saying it could not undo their losses.

Chinese prosecutors charged former security chief Zhou Yongkang with bribery, abuse of power and leaking state secrets, making him the highest-ranking Communist Party official to face corruption charges. The case is a landmark in President Xi Jinping’s anti-corruption campaign and will be tried in Tianjin.

A Philadelphia woman was charged after police said she abandoned her 21-year-old quadriplegic son with cerebral palsy in a park for more than four days while visiting her boyfriend in Maryland. The man was hospitalized with dehydration, malnutrition and other injuries; authorities are investigating his care history.

Walmart’s opposition to Arkansas’ religious freedom bill underscored growing business support for LGBT protections and pressured Gov. Asa Hutchinson to seek changes. The backlash in Arkansas and Indiana has put Republicans on the defensive as major companies warn such laws could enable discrimination.

A lapsed Catholic writer says Pope Francis’ welcoming tone and humility have rekindled her faith after years of alienation from the church. Newly appointed Cardinal Gerald Lacroix says Francis is rooted in the Gospel, emphasizing that the church may uphold doctrine without rejecting sinners.

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau and Vili Fualaau say they remain happily married nearly 10 years after wedding following her prison term for their relationship. The couple will discuss their marriage, her hopes to teach again and his struggles in an ABC “20/20” interview.

Hillary Clinton’s 2016 bid will be treated as a national test of gender equality, the article argues, placing a burden no male candidate faces. It says her victory or defeat should not be read as a referendum on women in politics, with partisanship and the economy likely to matter far more.

Amnesty International said governments are using terrorism and security fears to justify executions, citing Pakistan and China. Global executions fell 22% in 2014 to at least 607, but death sentences rose 28% to 2,466, driven by mass sentencings in countries such as Egypt and Nigeria.

Japan’s defense minister told parliament the Air Self Defense Force has never encountered a UFO believed to be extraterrestrial. He was responding to lawmaker and former wrestler Antonio Inoki, who asked whether jets had been scrambled over alien threats.

Mark Wahlberg will star in and produce “Patriots’ Day,” a film about the Boston Marathon bombing and the ensuing manhunt. The CBS Films project is expected to tell the story from the perspective of former Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis.

Martin O’Malley and Jim Webb courted Iowa Democrats as long-shot 2016 contenders facing Hillary Clinton’s dominant lead. O’Malley worked the room with polished retail politics, while Webb offered a more subdued pitch focused on governance, economic justice, criminal justice and veterans.

Turkish authorities arrested nine British citizens, including four children, at the Turkey-Syria border on suspicion of trying to cross illegally into Syria. Britain’s Foreign Office said it was seeking information from Turkish officials.

The DOJ indicted FedEx on drug-transport and money-laundering charges, alleging it knowingly shipped illegal online pharmacy orders despite warnings. FedEx denies liability, arguing common-carrier protections shield it from responsibility for package contents.

Kenyans mourned 147 people killed by Al-Shabaab at Garissa University College, sharing victims’ stories online under #147notjustanumber. Churches held emotional Easter tributes under armed guard, as authorities identified one attacker as the son of a local government official.

Swedish photographer Johan Bavman is documenting fathers who take extended parental leave under Sweden’s generous 480-day program. His project highlights bonding, exhaustion and shifting gender roles, even as only 12% of Swedish couples split leave equally.

Obama said he is committed to preserving Israel’s military edge and would stand by it if attacked, defending the Iran nuclear framework despite Netanyahu’s criticism. The deal would curb Iran’s nuclear program and expand inspections, with final talks due to continue until June 30.

Indiana’s new religious freedom law has reignited debate over whether such measures protect faith or enable discrimination. Similar federal and state laws have produced rare but notable cases involving religious minorities, from Native American eagle feathers and sacramental tea to kosher prison meals and Sikh ceremonial knives.

Five Chinese feminist activists detained ahead of International Women’s Day could face up to five years in prison on public order charges, their lawyer said. Their case has sparked international criticism and a “Free the Five” campaign, with rights groups saying their anti-harassment activism was lawful.

Selena’s family is developing “Selena the One,” a hologram-like digital version of the late Tejano star that can sing, dance and interact. The project aims to release new music and videos, collaborate with artists and tour in 2018, with crowdfunding set to begin April 16.

Former Rep. Michele Bachmann compared President Obama’s Iran diplomacy to the Germanwings co-pilot accused of deliberately crashing a passenger jet. The Facebook post drew sharp criticism as U.S.-Iran nuclear negotiations continued past a deadline.

Ryan Gosling’s directorial debut “Lost River” reaches theaters after a divisive Cannes premiere, drawing attention for its decaying Detroit setting. Gosling says the film grew from footage of the Brewster-Douglass Projects and aims to capture both the city’s ruin and resilience.

UK national Yahya Rashid, 19, was charged with terror offenses after being arrested at Luton airport on return from Istanbul. Police said the charges relate to alleged activity between November and March; he was due in Westminster Magistrates’ Court.

Mötley Crüe singer Vince Neil drew ridicule for a botched “Star-Spangled Banner” performance before a Las Vegas Outlaws game. The article compares his rendition with famous anthem highs and lows, from Whitney Houston’s acclaimed 1991 Super Bowl version to Roseanne Barr, Jimi Hendrix and Michael Bolton.

Nearly 2,000 World War I soldiers’ graffiti inscriptions have been found in a vast underground chalk quarry near Naours, France. Photographer Jeff Gusky says the site, used as refuge near the Somme battlefield, offers a rare human record of troops from Australia, Britain and the United States.

The Palestinian Authority formally joined the International Criminal Court, giving it jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories since June 2014. Israel and the United States opposed the move, while Palestinians and rights groups hailed it as a step toward justice.

Anthony Ray Hinton was freed after nearly 30 years on Alabama’s death row after prosecutors dropped murder charges tied to disputed firearms evidence. Hinton, who maintained his innocence, called his conviction a miscarriage of justice and thanked his lawyers and God.

Most Americans now see Tax Day as a payday, with refunds averaging nearly $3,000 and free filing easing the pain. But the author says the “happy ending” masks a tax system that favors capital and the wealthy while penalizing wage earners and some married couples.

Jordan Spieth retained control of the Masters after Saturday’s third round, taking a four-shot lead into Sunday despite late stumbles. Justin Rose moved to second at 12 under, with Phil Mickelson at 11 under and Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy back at six under.

New York prosecutors say Liana Barrientos married 10 times, sometimes within weeks, as part of an alleged immigration scam. She pleaded not guilty to filing false statements on a 2010 marriage license and faces up to four years in prison if convicted.

An Indiana pizzeria drew national backlash after its owners said they would refuse to cater a same-sex wedding, citing religious beliefs. Critics called for boycotts and police investigated threats against the restaurant, while supporters raised more than $842,000 for the business.

Mindy Kaling’s brother Vijay Chokalingam says he posed as Black to boost his medical school chances and criticize affirmative action. The article argues his stunt proves little about minority “privilege,” highlighting the discrimination he encountered and the continuing need for diversity in medicine.

Antarctica may have recorded its highest temperature ever, 63.5°F (15.5°C), at Argentina’s Esperanza Base on March 24. The World Meteorological Organization will review the measurement before making an official ruling later this year.

The Obama administration says it is no longer setting a timetable for an Iraqi-led assault to retake Mosul from ISIS. Officials cite the city’s size, strategic importance and the need to build Iraqi capacity, despite recent gains such as the recapture of Tikrit.

Paddy Power deleted and defended a tweet comparing Newcastle’s losses at Liverpool to police beatings of unarmed African-American men, prompting widespread criticism online. The betting firm said it was intended as a joke, but calls for accountability followed.

Philadelphia police added attempted murder to charges against Nyia Parler, accused of abandoning her quadriplegic son in woods for more than four days while she visited her boyfriend in Maryland. Parler remains in treatment in Maryland and cannot be extradited until it is completed, police said.

A South Korean man accused of stabbing U.S. Ambassador Mark Lippert in Seoul has been charged with attempted murder. Kim Ki-Jong, who opposed joint U.S.-South Korean military drills, also faces charges of assaulting a foreign envoy and business obstruction.
Jill Duggar Dillard, of TLC’s “19 Kids and Counting,” has given birth to her first child, a son named Israel David. The baby, born more than a week past his due date, weighed 9 pounds, 10 ounces.

"Furious 7" is on track for a $135 million-$138 million North American debut, the biggest opening since late 2013 and a record for April. The final film featuring Paul Walker could approach or top $300 million worldwide by Easter Sunday.

A Secret Service supervisor was placed on leave and had his security clearance suspended after a female employee accused him of assault following alleged unwanted sexual advances. The case, under inspector general review, adds to a string of scandals and security lapses at the agency.

Hillary Clinton is set to announce her 2016 presidential bid, entering as a highly experienced and formidable Democratic contender. But she faces challenges over authenticity, energizing the party base, defining her agenda, gender bias and the political liabilities tied to Bill Clinton.

The Justice Department is set to negotiate reforms to Ferguson’s police department after finding systemic racial discrimination and abusive court practices. Recent resignations and the election of two black city council members signal change, but activists say deeper structural reforms are needed.

Etihad Airways is searching for a missing cat that escaped after its carrier was damaged on a flight from Abu Dhabi to New York’s JFK airport. Owner Jennifer Stewart says the airline mishandled Felix, while Etihad says it is investigating and reviewing pet-handling procedures.

A South Carolina sailor was rescued off Virginia after drifting at sea for 66 days on a damaged sailboat. Louis Jordan survived storms, capsizings and scarce supplies by collecting rainwater and catching fish, and was found dehydrated but in surprisingly good condition.
